meta.title: Who really said "I've been around so long, I knew Doris Day before she was a virgin"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Groucho Marx. The joke is Oscar Levant’s, from his 1965 memoir — and he wrote it differently. The famous one-liner is a later paraphrase.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I've been around so long, I knew Doris Day before she was a virgin'?
meta.ogDescription: Oscar Levant, not Groucho — and Levant’s actual sentence names the film. The version people quote was tidied up by a 1972 anthology.

answer.label: Not Groucho Marx — actually Oscar Levant
answer.authorDates: 1906–1972 · American pianist, composer, actor and professional wit
answer.sourceLine: The joke is Levant’s, and he told it about a film he was in. Wikiquote’s sourced Levant entry ↗ gives the sentence from The Memoirs of an Amnesiac (1965): “My last picture for Warners was Romance on the High Seas. It was Doris Day’s first picture; that was before she became a virgin.” The same entry identifies the compressed “I knew Doris Day before she was a virgin” as a later paraphrase, printed in Max Wilk’s The Wit and Wisdom of Hollywood (1972). Wikiquote’s Groucho page ↗ lists the Marx version under Misattributed and sends the reader to Levant.

source.excerpt: My last picture for Warners was Romance on the High Seas. It was Doris Day’s first picture; that was before she became a virgin.
trail: Wikiquote’s Oscar Levant page ↗ carries the sentence in its sourced section, not among unsourced attributions, and cites The Memoirs of an Amnesiac (1965) at p. 192. Immediately beneath it the page states that “a later paraphrase of this appeared in The Wit and Wisdom of Hollywood (1972) by Max Wilk: ‘I knew Doris Day before she was a virgin.’”

Wikiquote’s Groucho Marx page ↗ lists the Groucho form under Misattributed with the note that it was “apparently said by Oscar Levant”, citing the same Wilk anthology. Two separate Wikiquote pages, maintained for two different people, agree on where the joke belongs.

The bibliographic details check out against the library record: the Internet Archive’s catalogue entry for The Memoirs of an Amnesiac ↗ gives the author as Levant, Oscar, 1906–1972, published New York: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1965, LCCN 65010856. The book is lending-restricted, so we have confirmed the edition rather than read the page.

The setting is verifiable too. Wikipedia’s article on Romance on the High Seas ↗ records it as a 1948 Warner Bros. musical directed by Michael Curtiz, featuring Doris Day “in her film debut”, with Oscar Levant in the cast as Oscar Farrar — exactly the arrangement Levant’s sentence describes.
source.excerptNote: Levant’s own version is the better joke, because it is anchored. He is not making a general remark about a screen persona — he is saying he watched it being installed, from the next chair on the same set. Romance on the High Seas really was Day’s film debut and Levant really was in it, which is what gives the line its standing.

source.rightsNote: The documented wording comes from The Memoirs of an Amnesiac, published by G. P. Putnam’s Sons in New York in 1965 — far too recent for the public domain in the United States, where protection attaches to anything first published from 1931 onward. The shorter paraphrase is later still, first recorded in a 1972 anthology, and carries no better claim to being free.

author.name: Oscar Levant
author.heading: About Oscar Levant
author.metaLine: 1906–1972 · American pianist, composer, actor and radio wit
author.bio: Oscar Levant was a serious concert pianist — the foremost interpreter of his friend George Gershwin — who became far more famous for talking. On radio panel shows and in films he perfected a character built from neurosis, insomnia and unbearable candour, and then wrote three memoirs in the same voice, of which The Memoirs of an Amnesiac (1965) is the best known. His jokes were mordant enough that they have a habit of being reassigned to comedians who could not have been in the room: the Doris Day line is about a film Levant himself appeared in.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: One of the most-quoted Hollywood put-downs, credited to the wrong wit and quoted in words nobody wrote.

items.why: Wikiquote ↗ files the line under Misattributed for Marx and says flatly that it was “apparently said by Oscar Levant”. No Groucho source carries it, and the joke depends on having been on the Warner Bros. lot in 1948 — which Levant was and Marx was not.
Wikiquote’s sourced Levant entry ↗ quotes it from The Memoirs of an Amnesiac (1965), and the joke fits the facts: Romance on the High Seas ↗ was Doris Day’s film debut and Levant was in its cast.

Levant wrote two sentences naming a film. Wikiquote records the compressed “I knew Doris Day before she was a virgin” as a later paraphrase from Max Wilk’s The Wit and Wisdom of Hollywood (1972). The opening clause people now attach to it — “I’ve been around so long” — appears in neither documented source; it was added somewhere in circulation, and we could not find where.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is Oscar Levant’s ↗, from his 1965 memoir, about a film he was in — and the famous short version is a 1972 anthology’s tidying-up, not his sentence.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The joke is a very precise piece of industry knowledge. Doris Day was not a virginal person; she was a working singer on her fourth marriage by the time the image hardened, and the studio built the wholesome persona around her over several pictures. Levant is claiming to have been present before the construction started — which, having played opposite her in her first film, he was.

That is what makes the drift to Groucho a real loss rather than a footnote. Coming from Marx it is a generic crack about a famous prude. Coming from Levant it is a colleague pointing at a manufactured image and saying he watched it get made.
detailsBody: Levant’s lines drift more than most, and the reason is structural. He was famous for saying things rather than for writing them down, so much of his best material reached the public through anthologies and other people’s memoirs — formats that compress, tidy and occasionally reassign. The three books he did write are the corrective, which is exactly why the 1965 memoir settles this one.
context.pull: Not a joke about a prude — a joke about a persona being manufactured.
